steps.label: Boosting and AdaBoost
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp25 with view-from-text-v2: the pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic, with the terms defined inside the same figure. 7 main pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). The experiments on pages 1, 5, 6 and 7 (20-dimensional two-class Gaussians, stumps, flipped labels) were designed for this lecture and generated by code; page 5 redoes the source's Example 4.3. The source contributes the derivation of the weights and α, the algorithm, the margin explanation with the criticism that the bound is loose, and the conclusion that it is no panacea. The 5-run mean for clean labels at 500 rounds is exactly 5.75% and is written 5.8% by rounding (the lecture said 5.7% and was corrected). English version.

steps.label: Weak to strong
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP25, following the combining of classifiers in KP24. The question: can a weak classifier that is only a little better than guessing be boosted into a strong one? The experiment was designed for this lecture and generated by code: 20-dimensional two-class Gaussians, each component standard normal plus the class mean minus or plus a, with a equal to 2 over the square root of 20; 200 training points and 400 test points. The weak classifiers are 20 stumps asking whether x j is above 0. Each dot in the figure is the test error of one stump; they lie between 27% and 36%, mean 31.6%, all below the 50% guessing line but only a little. Three cards on the right: a weak classifier is one whose error is only a little below guessing; a stump is a tree with one question on one feature; the boosting mechanism is that each round changes the sample weights, putting more weight on the hardest, misclassified points, and the final vote is weighted. The next page asks where the sample weights come from.

steps.label: Where weights come from
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed 20 stumps, each only a little better than guessing. This page asks where the sample weights come from in boosting. First two terms: stage-wise optimisation optimises only the newly added classifier and freezes the earlier ones, F m equals F m minus 1 plus alpha m times phi m; the exponential loss is e to the minus z, with z equal to y times F of x: a small penalty for z above 0, right, and a heavy one for z below 0, wrong. Four steps: the goal is the sum of the exponential loss; split F m, so the exponential of a sum becomes the product of two exponentials, one containing only the earlier F m minus 1 and one containing the new alpha and phi; name the first one w i, equal to e to the minus y i times F m minus 1; then the loss becomes the sum of w i times e to the minus y alpha phi. w i contains neither alpha nor phi: it is the sample weight, and the larger it is the harder the point; so phi m must minimise the weighted error P m with the weights normalised to sum 1. The next page asks how large a voice each weak classifier should get.

steps.label: The voice α
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the exponential loss splits stage by stage and w is the sample weight. This page asks how large a voice each weak classifier should get. Split the loss J into two groups, right and wrong: the weights of the right points sum to 1 minus P, each multiplied by e to the minus alpha; the weights of the wrong points sum to P, each multiplied by e to the alpha. So J of alpha equals e to the minus alpha times 1 minus P plus e to the alpha times P. Setting the derivative to zero: minus e to the minus alpha times 1 minus P plus e to the alpha times P equals 0, giving alpha equal to one half ln of 1 minus P over P. In the figure the horizontal axis is the weighted error P and the vertical axis alpha, with four marked points: 1.099 at P equal to 0.1, 0.424 at 0.3, 0 at 0.5 and minus 0.424 at 0.7. A very accurate classifier gets a large voice, guessing gets 0, and one worse than guessing, P above 0.5, gets a negative alpha and its answer is used reversed. The next page asks how the sample weights change after one round.

steps.label: Weight update
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the voice alpha comes from the right and wrong weights in two groups. This page asks how the sample weights change after one round. The update is w i times e to the minus y alpha phi, divided by Z; wrong points grow and right points shrink. The hand example was designed for this lecture: 10 points of 0.1 each, with phi wrong on 3 of them. Step 1: P is 0.3 and alpha is one half ln of 0.7 over 0.3, which is 0.4236. Step 2: the wrong ones are multiplied by e to the alpha, 1.5275, so 0.1 becomes 0.1528; the right ones by e to the minus alpha, 0.6547, so 0.1 becomes 0.0655. Step 3: Z is 3 times 0.1528 plus 7 times 0.0655, which is 0.9165; after normalising each wrong one is 0.1667 and each right one 0.0714. In the figure grey is before the update and colour is after. The three wrong ones together are 3 times 0.1667, which is 0.5: the next phi must look after them first. The next page asks how the training and test errors behave when this update is repeated.

steps.label: Algorithm and error curves
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that wrong points grow and the 3 wrong ones together hold 0.5. This page asks how the training and test errors behave when this update is repeated. AdaBoost in three steps: start with w i equal to 1 over N; repeat, find phi m minimising P m, compute alpha m and update w i; finally f of x is the sign of the sum of alpha k times phi k. The setup redoes the source's Example 4.3 for this lecture: the same 20-dimensional two-class Gaussians, 200 training and 400 test points, and each round picks from 20 features and all thresholds the stump with the smallest weighted error, for 2000 rounds. In the figure the horizontal axis is the rounds on a log scale; blue is the training error and red the test error. Round 1 has training 25.5% and test 28.75%, better than the 31.6% mean of a random stump. The green line is round 17, from which the training error is 0; the test error keeps falling afterwards: 12.25% at round 10, 4.75% at round 50, 3.25% at round 200, and levels near 4% after about 200 rounds; with 400 test points 1% is only 4 points, so the levelling is within sampling error. The next page asks why the test error does not rise.

steps.label: The margin view
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that after the training error reaches 0 the test error still falls to about 4%. This page asks why the test error does not rise. The normalised margin is y times F of x divided by the sum of the alphas, lying between minus 1 and 1; positive means right and larger means more confident. The source's bound says the generalisation error is roughly at most the probability that the margin is below gamma plus a term independent of the number of rounds K, which is the source of the resistance. The experiment was designed for this lecture and uses the data and model of the previous page: the minimum margin rises with the rounds, minus 1.000 at round 1, minus 0.205 at round 10, plus 0.148 at round 50, 0.179 at round 100, 0.203 at round 200 and 0.220 at round 2000; the share of margins below 0.1 falls from 25.5% to 0%. As the rounds increase the minimum margin is pushed up, which is a qualitative explanation of why the test error does not rise after the training error reaches 0. The limit is the source's criticism: the bound is very loose, unless N is in the tens of thousands, so it is only a qualitative explanation; stage-wise optimisation is itself an implicit regularisation. The next page asks whether AdaBoost never overfits.

steps.label: No panacea
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the minimum margin keeps rising and the test error does not rise after the training error reaches 0. This page asks whether AdaBoost never overfits. The experiment was designed for this lecture: the same kind of data, training labels flipped at random at 15%, test labels clean; 0% and 15% are each run 5 times with fresh samples, training seeds 10 to 14 and test seeds 50 to 54, and averaged, so the numbers differ from the earlier single run; every round uses the best stump, for 2000 rounds. In the figure the green line has clean labels and falls steadily to 5.5%; the red line has 15% flipped, lowest at about 30 rounds with 17.8% (a round-by-round sweep gives about 16.5% at round 36) and then rises to 23.3%. With clean labels the errors at rounds 10, 100, 500 and 2000 are 14.4%, 6.6%, 5.8% and 5.5%; the 5-run mean at 500 rounds is exactly 5.75%, written 5.8% by rounding, and the lecture's earlier 5.7% was corrected. A possible cause: the exponential loss punishes badly placed samples too heavily; after 2000 rounds the 15.5% flipped samples hold 36% of the weight in one of the runs. The common myth is that AdaBoost never overfits; on hard tasks with a high Bayes error and noisy labels it can degrade sharply, which is the source's conclusion. This is the last page of the main line. The next page is an extension: what does a negative alpha mean?

steps.label: Extension: negative α
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that with 15% flipped labels the test error rises after about 30 rounds. This extension page returns to alpha: what does a negative alpha mean for a classifier worse than guessing? With P equal to 0.7, alpha is one half ln of 0.3 over 0.7, which is minus 0.4236. Minus 0.4236 times phi equals plus 0.4236 times minus phi, and minus phi has weighted error 0.3, so it is a good classifier. For the weight update: points phi gets wrong are multiplied by e to the minus 0.4236, 0.6547, and shrink; points it gets right are multiplied by 1.5275 and grow, exactly as for the reversed classifier. So for a classifier worse than guessing, a negative alpha simply uses its answer reversed. The next page has two exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that a negative alpha uses the classifier reversed. This page is the exercises. Exercise 1: 5 samples with weight 0.2 each, phi gets 1 wrong, and the weighted error P is 0.2; what is alpha? The hint is alpha equal to one half ln of 1 minus P over P. Exercise 2: after updating and normalising, what is the weight of each sample? The hint is that wrong ones are multiplied by e to the alpha and right ones by e to the minus alpha, then divided by Z. Work them out first; the next page is the worked solution.

steps.label: Extension: worked solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page set two exercises. Exercise 1: alpha is one half ln of 0.8 over 0.2, which is one half ln 4, which is 0.6931; e to the alpha is 2 and e to the minus alpha is 0.5. Exercise 2: the wrong one 0.2 times 2 is 0.4; each of the 4 right ones 0.2 times 0.5 is 0.1; Z is 0.4 plus 4 times 0.1, which is 0.8. Normalised: the wrong one 0.4 over 0.8 is 0.5 and each right one 0.1 over 0.8 is 0.125. Check: 0.5 plus 4 times 0.125 is 1. The wrong point holds exactly half, the same rule as the 3 points holding 0.5 on page 4: after the update the weights the old phi gets wrong always sum to 0.5, the old phi's weighted error becomes 0.5, so a new phi is needed. This is the last page of KP25; the next KP is the following unit of chapter 4.
